prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The depth map shows a tiered indoor lounge layout with a seated person on the immediate right (bright white, ~0.4–0.7 m away) holding a smartphone in both hands within both their own and the camera wearer's arm's reach, an empty armchair with two throw pillows in the middle ground ahead (~1.8–2.5 m away, roughly 1.5 m beyond the seated person), a floor lamp pole and another chair armrest between them (~1.0–2.2 m), and a wall with windows on the left (~2.5–3.5 m) leading to a deeper background room on the upper right (>4 m). The person on the right is heavily cropped by the right and bottom frame edges, faces left in profile toward their phone rather than toward the camera wearer, and shifts slightly backward or out of the upper-right frame in frames 3 and 4 as the camera pitches slightly down and left before returning in frame 5. Theperson's arms and phone partially occlude the foreground chair armrest and the lower right corner of the middle-ground armchair, while the middle-ground armchair and lamp pole partially occlude the background room. Compared to the RGB strip, the depth map clearly separates the foreground person, the intermediate chair armrest, the middle-ground armchair, and the thin vertical lamp pole into distinct distance planes. However, it is unreliable on the exterior trees seen through the left windows—rendering them at the same flat indoor depth (~3 m) as the window wall—and loses the thin dark metal legs of the armchair and foreground glass table surface into the floor gradient.
descriptions.segmentation: The segmentation map isolates the central armchair (labelled 'couch' in yellow, ~1.8–2.5 m ahead), the foreground chair armrest on the lower right (labelled 'chair', ~1.0–1.2 m), the small potted plant on the left windowsill (~2.8 m away and ~1.5 m left of the armchair), and a distant armchair in the back-right room (labelled 'couch' or 'bed', ~4.5–5.5 m away). It also intermittently masks the seated person on the bottom right (tan/brown mask in frames 1, 2, and 4 at ~0.4–0.7 m) and the handheld smartphone within their hands (grey mask in frame 4 at ~0.6 m), showing how the foreground armrest and person overlap in front of the lower-right corner of the central armchair. Across the 5 frames, the masks shift slightly horizontally and vertically with the camera wearer's minor head tilt, while the far-right background chair disappears behind the right frame boundary in frames 3 and 4 when the camera turns slightly left. While the segmentation map helps group the central armchair and its two pillows into a single coherent object mass and picks out the small windowsill plant and distant background chair against complex lighting, it is highly unreliable in class labels and temporal consistency. Specifically, it mislabels the central and distant armchairs as 'couch' or 'bed', mislabels the smartphone as 'chair'/'remote' in frame 4, completely misses the person's upper head at the top right, drops the person's body mask entirely in frames 3 and 5, and hallucinates a 'potted plant' on the decorative box on the low left table (~1.8 m away) in frame 3.
descriptions.pose: The pose map is almost completely blank across all five frames, detecting only a small, miniature 2D body skeleton (yellow) in the lower-left quadrant of frame 2 at the location of the smartphone screen (~0.6 m from the camera wearer) and no magenta hand skeletons anywhere. This single skeleton corresponds to a tiny full-body figure displayed on the screen of the phone held by the person on the right, oriented upright and facing forward/slightly right on the display, while the actual person sitting ~0.4–0.7 m to the right of the camera wearer is completely unrepresented. Because the real person's body is severely truncated by the bottom and right edges of the egocentric frame—leaving only their nose/chin in profile at the top right, a sliver of patterned shirt on the lower right, and two hands holding the phone at the bottom—the pose estimator fails to detect their torso, head, or hands in any of the 5 frames. Although the pose map highlights the presence of a human figure on the darkly lit smartphone screen in frame 2 that is tiny and hard to notice at a glance in the RGB image, it is entirely unreliable for scene-level spatial understanding, missing the nearby person and their within-reach hands across the entire sequence.
